paragraphs: One-line judgment: audio and video technicians are not about "flipping a switch and getting picture and sound", but about turning event or recording requirements into a verifiable equipment list, signal flow, test results, operating status, and handover at strike; people who just want to get the show started as quickly as possible and are unwilling to verify channels, power, and rigging status segment by segment are not suited to it.

Signals to keep exploring: you can draw the signal flow clearly and troubleshoot segment by segment (microphone → mixing console → processor → amplifier → speaker, or camera → switcher → recording and broadcast), report status accurately during a countdown with multiple people, are willing to cut power, verify the absence of voltage, and confirm rigging and load before operating, and stop and escalate when connections, power, or rigging status are unclear.

Conditions to pause investment first: you have not yet completed a full setup, test, and strike process under any supervised conditions, or you can only explain your interest by "liking equipment"; also, do not treat course grades, one volunteer favor, or knowing one software program as proof that you can work on live electrical parts, climb and rig at height, or serve as the main control operator for an event. Work involving electricity, rigging, and work at height must be carried out by personnel with the corresponding authorization and protective conditions according to procedure, and this page does not provide on-site work instructions.

Education and authority must be verified separately: O*NET lists 27-4011.00 as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0), and among respondents 43% believe a bachelor's degree is required, 25% believe a high school diploma or equivalent is required, and 20% believe a postsecondary certificate is required; the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists this occupational group as usually requiring postsecondary education with short-term on-the-job training. Coursework, equipment operating proficiency, internal institutional qualification, authorization for work on live electrical parts and for work at height and rigging, and authority for external broadcast or live streaming are different statuses, and must be verified item by item according to employer, position, and location; this page does not provide electrical, rigging, or on-site response instructions.

One line: this is an occupation that turns live or recorded audio and video requirements into verifiable equipment and signal chains, with the core being setup, testing, operation, troubleshooting, and strike, and responsibility for connections, power, rigging, and records, rather than an interest in gear or proficiency with a single software program.

The work of audio and video technicians can be divided into three categories: setup and configuration tasks (listing microphones, speakers, cables and connectors, mixing consoles, cameras, monitors, and servers according to the event or recording requirements, connecting them and verifying the signal flow and channels, and testing segment by segment and recording the results); operation and troubleshooting tasks (verifying inputs and channels against the rundown, monitoring picture and sound quality, localizing anomalies to a specific stage, switching or replacing equipment according to contingency plans, and recording the handling process); and strike and handover tasks (cutting power, disconnecting, counting, and packing according to the checklist, recording damage and missing items, and handing over the venue and equipment status). All three categories are premised on stopping and escalating when connections, power, rigging, or equipment status are unclear.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET 27-4011.00 Audio and Video Technicians (page updated in 2026). The official duties are to set up, maintain, and dismantle audio and video equipment; there are 31 official tasks, and the page lists the first few by importance: notify supervisors when major equipment repairs are needed (77), diagnose and resolve media system problems (71), direct and coordinate assistants and other personnel during production (68), compress, digitize, duplicate, and store audio and video data (68), install, adjust, and operate recording and transmission equipment (67), control lighting and sound at live events (65), monitor incoming and outgoing picture and sound signals (66), and mix and adjust (65), with operating drones for aerial footage and purchasing audio and video equipment as newly listed tasks. Field boundaries: the task list describes group work and does not mean every position carries out all tasks. The details numbers are Importance, with 66 monitoring and 65 mixing marked Supplemental, not frequency or a threshold for each person; the drone task does not provide flight permission, and the actual rules are verified separately.

entries.answer: They list the microphones, speakers, cables and connectors, mixing consoles, cameras, monitors, and servers needed for the event or recording and complete the connections, verifying the signal flow and channels and testing segment by segment; during the event or recording they monitor picture and sound quality, localize anomalies to a specific stage, and switch or replace according to the contingency plan; and afterward they cut power, disconnect, count, and pack according to the checklist, record damage and missing items, and hand over the venue status. It is not simply "flipping a switch", but closing the equipment list, signal flow, test results, and handover status into a chain of responsibility.
entries.question: What do audio and video technicians do every day?

entries.answer: Mainly live electrical work and electrical hazards, height and rigging risks, signal interruption and operational failure, equipment damage and inventory errors, work beyond authority and unclear work permits, and missing records and unclear responsibility. On the U.S. side, see OSHA 29 CFR 1910.303 for the installation and use of electrical equipment; live electrical work, height work, and rigging must be carried out by personnel with authorization and protective conditions according to procedure, and when conditions are unclear you must stop and escalate.
entries.question: What risks does this job most need to be watched for in advance?

entries.answer: Look at observable behavior: whether you can draw the signal flow clearly, count and connect according to the checklist, test segment by segment and record the results, report status accurately during a countdown with multiple people, and record outstanding items truthfully and stop to escalate when connections, power, rigging, or work permits are unclear. O*NET lists the interest code for this occupation as RC (Realistic + Conventional), but a matching interest only indicates a similar direction and cannot replace signal principles, testing and troubleshooting ability, and safety awareness.

subject.summary: Audio and video technicians set up, test, operate, and dismantle audio and video equipment for events or recordings, verify the signal chain segment by segment, record changes, and stop and escalate when connections, power, rigging, or equipment status are unclear. On the U.S. side this corresponds to O*NET 27-4011.00 (Audio and Video Technicians), in Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0), with education mostly at the postsecondary level; Mainland China statistics are aggregated by industry category, do not list this occupation separately, and do not cover overtime pay, performance allowances, or project payments.
